content: Lassa fever is an acute viral hemorrhagic illness caused by the Lassa virus, which is a zoonotic, single-stranded RNA virus. The primary vector for transmission to humans is the Mastomys natalensis rodent, commonly known as the multimammate rat. This rodent sheds the virus in its urine and feces, which can contaminate food, water, or surfaces. Lassa fever is endemic to West Africa, with an estimated annual incidence of 300,000 to 500,000 cases and a case fatality rate ranging from 5% to 15%. During outbreaks, the fatality rate can rise significantly, sometimes reaching as high as 65%. Individuals at higher risk of contracting Lassa fever include those who travel to endemic regions, individuals exposed to infected rodents or humans, and healthcare workers who may come into contact with infected bodily fluids. Pregnant women, immunosuppressed individuals, and young children are particularly vulnerable to severe complications associated with the disease. Many infected individuals remain asymptomatic or experience only mild symptoms. However, symptomatic patients often present initially with persistent high-grade fever and other non-specific symptoms such as headache, muscle pain, and fatigue. If untreated, most cases resolve spontaneously, but in some instances, the disease progresses to more severe manifestations. These may include hemorrhage, deafness, edema, seizures, coma, and even death. The pathophysiology of Lassa fever involves the virus infecting endothelial cells and replicating intracellularly. The Lassa virus uses an L-polymerase enzyme and nucleocapsid protein (NP) to synthesize ribonucleoprotein (RNP), which produces mRNA and antigenomic RNA necessary for viral replication. The NP protein also plays a role in evading the host immune response. This viral activity leads to vascular dysfunction, which underlies many of the clinical symptoms. While the virus can infect multiple organs, the liver is a common target, and hepatitis or hepatic necrosis is a frequent complication. The diagnosis of Lassa fever is typically confirmed by detecting Lassa-specific IgG antibodies in the patient’s serum using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Other diagnostic methods include reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and immunohistochemistry, which can be performed on tissue samples such as skin or liver. Laboratory findings may also reveal evidence of organ damage or complications, which require close monitoring. The treatment of Lassa fever primarily involves the administration of the antiviral drug ribavirin. Intravenous ribavirin is most effective when given early in the disease course, ideally within the first six days of symptom onset. The recommended regimen includes an initial loading dose of 30 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 2 g), followed by 16 mg/kg (up to 1 g) every six hours for four days, and then 8 mg/kg (up to 500 mg) every eight hours for six days. Supportive care is also critical and includes maintaining respiratory function, as well as ensuring proper fluid and electrolyte balance. There is currently no vaccine available for Lassa fever. The natural history of Lassa fever varies widely. While many cases are mild or asymptomatic, severe cases can lead to complications such as neurosensory deafness, hypovolemic shock, and fulminant hepatic necrosis. Prognosis is generally favorable for mild cases, but the presence of complications, pregnancy, infancy, or immunosuppression is associated with a poorer outcome and increased mortality risk.
